Amazon plays catch-up with Alexa generative AI, shows off refreshed hardware
Alexa will converse more naturally next year, losing its robotic tone of nearly a decade, and answer questions like the start time for football games and recipe ideas. It will also be able to compose and recite poems, Amazon showed at the company's annual product launch in Arlington, Virginia.
By Greg Bensinger
Amazon.com Inc on Wednesday unveiled a slate of new and refreshed devices and updated its Alexa voice assistant with generative artificial intelligence to attract users to the unprofitable product as competition grows from chatbots like Google's Bard.
Alexa will converse more naturally next year, losing its robotic tone of nearly a decade, and answer questions like the start time for football games and recipe ideas. It will also be able to compose and recite poems, Amazon showed at the company's annual product launch in Arlington, Virginia.
Amazon introduced Alexa in 2014, but has not found a consistent means to make it profitable, instead driving shoppers toward the company's website for more purchases.
The Seattle-based company has worked to pep up Alexa particularly after OpenAI's ChatGPT burst on the scene in November with longform answers to complex queries. Similar chatbots sparked an investor frenzy in generative AI startups.
On Tuesday, Reuters reported that morale among workers in Amazon's Lab126 hardware unit has suffered over shifting strategies and concerns that the company is not producing popular consumer devices. Many products under development, people familiar with matter told Reuters, are meant to put Alexa in more rooms of the home, such as a carbon monoxide detector with the service built in.
At the event, Amazon also introduced refreshed versions of children's Fire tablets, the Show (an Echo with a screen), a speaker for televisions and new search capabilities on the FireTV service to find free content.

text:

Chip packaging is the next battleground for tech lead: CEO, Cadence Design Systems
Sophisticated chip packaging helped Nvidia Corp. develop industry-leading AI accelerators, but limited suppliers are now proving a bottleneck for the US company.
The US should invest more in cutting-edge semiconductor packaging to ensure it leads in emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, Cadence Design Systems Inc. Chief Executive Officer Anirudh Devgan said.
Sophisticated chip packaging helped Nvidia Corp. develop industry-leading AI accelerators, but limited suppliers are now proving a bottleneck for the US company. As computing demands grow and advanced chips get more expensive to make as the transistors get smaller, assembling silicon into three-dimensional structures and working around physical limitations are becoming essential.
“Manufacturing is critical, three nanometer, two nanometer, but you also have to invest where the puck is going. The puck is going to 3D-IC,” Devgan told Bloomberg News in an interview in Taipei. His firm is one of the three leading semiconductor design software providers in the world, and it counts Nvidia and other AI hardware developers among its customers.
The stacking of so-called chiplets into a multifunctional 3D chip is one of the ways that silicon designers are advancing their capabilities as the constant pursuit of ever-smaller transistors approaches the limits of physics. It’s helping create chips powerful enough to compute workloads like generative AI, and to do so at a reasonable cost. Securing a lead on that front should be a priority for the US, the CEO of San Jose, California-based Cadence said.
“You don’t need to even own a fab to do packaging because sometimes you can have chips from different fabs assembled. For the US government, it’s good to have this kind of technology,” Devgan said.
The Nvidia case offers an illustration, as the company has a clear technological edge on the rest of the industry, but it’s supply-constrained by limited capacity provided by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., its chipmaker of choice for advanced AI parts. At Semicon Taiwan last week, TSMC Chairman Mark Liu reaffirmed the company’s view that the shortage will persist for another 18 months, after Nvidia said in late August that it’s happy with the progress it’s making in getting more components.
Cadence’s software is an indispensable design tool for semiconductor firms large and small. Its critical role in the global chip industry was highlighted by the US Department of Commerce putting export controls on design software for cutting-edge semiconductors last year as part of measures to cut off China’s access to advanced technologies.
The company is looking into applying for funding from the USD 52 billion Chips and Science Act, Devgan said, which was passed last year to help bring more of the global semiconductor supply chain within US borders.

title: Council Post: A New Lifeline: How AI Can Change Healthcare For The Better
text:
Ethan Davidoff, Founder and CEO, Atlas Health.
In 2021, more than 8% of the American public had no form of health insurance. Yet that same year, U.S. healthcare spending reached $4.3 trillion—or a dizzying total of about $13,000 per person. Even more, over 40% of U.S. families say they’ve incurred sizable medical debt, and nearly a quarter of them report being late or unable to pay it off. Given these access and affordability challenges, more Americans are disillusioned with such a complex system.
Patients certainly shouldn’t be stuck with this massive financial burden. Fortunately, artificial intelligence (AI) is turning the tide by helping providers and administrators across the care continuum with everything from patient intake and medical billing to treatment. It can also help level the proverbial playing field—as AI algorithms can help avoid human bias, improving patient services along with access to care.
I believe that this degree of positive momentum will inevitably change healthcare for the better. In this article, I’ll explore some of the most compelling AI use cases industry-wide, all of which help liberate patients and providers from burdensome tasks and make healthcare more accessible and efficient.
Interactive Medical Assistants
Telehealth usage exploded during the pandemic and continues to be widely utilized. Twenty-two percent of adults reported that they were still using it toward the end of 2022. Now, conversational AI can serve as an effective, patient-facing medical “assistant” to help streamline this process. Where providers may have once needed to join a video conference to answer very preliminary health questions, AI can now absorb this task, serving as an early screening tool to triage the severity of a case.
Medical professionals can turn to AI to complement in-person care to help craft treatment plans or as an initial research tool to aid in their diagnostics. Conversational AI tools can use proven, validated scientific findings (via deep learning) to answer specific health questions and guide patients on a potential path toward treatment. At the prescribing stage, however, providers would step in for critical and more nuanced conversations.
Some research has shown that there’s significant potential for patient trust in AI chatbots. In fact, 47% of patients recently polled indicated that they’d consider an early consultation with AI versus a physician. The same survey suggests that patients will also grow more inclined to consult AI once it’s been validated by a trusted provider. In the process, it becomes a useful patient-care resource but not a replacement for direct treatment.
Enabling Access
AI has the potential to democratize medical information and enable health systems to access reliable and relevant data. It can also analyze vast amounts of data quickly and accurately. This makes it ideally suited to help solve data-related challenges across healthcare access and affordability. AI is already being used in this way to simplify the complex financial assistance landscape and make treatments more accessible to many patients.
There are thousands of financial assistance programs available to help patients afford their medical bills. The problem is that they all have their own eligibility criteria, application forms and enrollment periods. At the same time, a patient’s eligibility status is constantly changing based on factors like employment, place of residence, diagnoses and prescribed medication. This makes identifying matching programs and submitting applications a burdensome task for patients—and even for patient advocates who are dedicated to helping patients with financial assistance every day.
The use of predictive analytics and machine learning helps keep track of program criteria and ever-changing patient eligibility factors to ensure patients are matched with all eligible programs. This makes optimal (and particularly high-cost) treatment more accessible for many patients. This type of work would normally take advocates hours and even days to do, but by leveraging AI, they can quickly help more patients access the life-saving treatment they need.
Administrative Efficiencies, User Experience And Future Use
AI can populate forms with patient profile information and medical history data, cutting down on the time it takes for providers to conduct research and related data entry, more quickly creating a full “view” of the patient. This view, which would lack human errors or omissions, could help inform the critical decisions that providers make and give them more time to dedicate to their patients.
Overall, I envision AI radically up-leveling care and operations across today’s enormous health network. It can help teams aggregate and assess data and make more informed decisions off that data. Even AI’s back-office benefits can create process efficiencies that equate to more provider time with a patient with positive downstream effects.
We’re still in AI’s infancy, but I’m adamant about its potential. I believe that it will become a part of the healthcare industry at every level, helping patients as they schedule, clear financial hurdles, receive treatment, recover and focus on prevention to live healthier lives. AI adopters across the healthcare community are positioned to lead the way in contributing to a better and more equitable experience for patients.

title: Council Post: As AI’s Profile Grows, Defining Guardrails Will Be Key To Effective Adoption
text:
Pete Lamson is the CEO of Employ Inc., a leading solutions provider that empowers companies to overcome their recruiting and TA challenges.
The world is buzzing about the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to change the game in business. It’s helping professionals across industries and departments in new and exciting ways, freeing up time for strategic thinking while automating and optimizing workflows—and leaders are all in on supporting that cause.
Enterprises have spent considerable sums to fold new AI tools and applications into their digital ecosystems at lightning speed, both to enhance their internal workflows and the products they offer to their customers. But are they succeeding?
Sure, sometimes. But more often, they’re not.
The trend of adopting or adding these features to stay current, as many companies are choosing to do, may not be the best path forward. Though early adoption has its benefits to pursuits that rely on data and experience to bolster efficacy, it also comes with some significant risks. That’s particularly true for today’s unproven and often unprotected AI tools.
Like any other emerging technology, AI is a tool—not a cure-all. It enables companies to take advantage of opportunities; nothing more, nothing less. Leaders hoping to ride the AI wave to long-term success will need to take a measured approach to adoption. As they did with the internet and smartphones before, executives and managers will need to start outlining thoughtful strategies for AI, as well as limits for its use that address the needs of employees in roles such as customer service, sales, product design and more.
Growing Risk
With the broad potential of tools in the space and the technology’s capabilities evolving at lightning speed, developing and implementing high-level policies around the use of AI in workplaces will be a critical undertaking in the coming months and years. Failing to do so will put businesses at significant risk, as adoption without direction often does.
The primary risk for companies folding open-access generative AI tools (like ChatGPT and Bard) into their processes is increased exposure. For example, leaking data. Open-access tools often store user inputs on servers that can be (and have been) accessed by bad actors or through glitches in the sites. That means code, confidential announcements, protected user data and anything else your team may think to run through the system could be there for the taking.
Of course, that’s not the only danger associated with accessibility. Generative AI tools often learn from user inputs, which can affect the quality of the results. If employees are not educated about the possibility of generative AI tools returning invalid, inaccurate or subpar outputs, it may result in reputational exposure for the company—both in terms of client work and on a broader scale.
Companies that lean too heavily on AI in their interactions with clients or even to produce materials for client use may risk losing contracts if deliverables contain factual flaws or clients catch on that generative AI is doing the heavy lifting. Of course, the risk can go far beyond reputation and client retention. It can create legal issues as well. Despite the relatively short time the technology has been in wide use, American courts have already seen defamation cases, potential sanctions against lawyers and copyright suits related to ChatGPT.
The above just scratches the surface, though. As time goes on, new risks and rewards will emerge, and it’s up to executives and managers to stay ahead of that development and outline and implement best practices throughout their organizations that balance progress and protections.
Getting It Right
With AI’s capabilities—and limitations—quickly becoming clear, leaders who proceed with caution will be more likely to succeed than those who adopt tools for the sake of adoption. It’s critical that leaders get ahead of the curve in defining best practices and guidance around AI in different contexts.
Outlining guardrails for the use of AI and its integration into a company’s ecosystem will be a challenging process, and it's certain to be an ongoing one. To do it right, businesses will need to:
• Define the vision: The process begins at the top, with executive leadership developing an enterprise-wide mandate for AI’s role and the opportunities it presents. They can use this as a guiding light to develop a tangible and executable AI strategy that addresses both internal operations and the services and experiences the business offers to customers.
• Learn the landscape: Once the strategy is defined, leaders should explore the available tools with an open mind. That means ignoring headlines about the “next best thing” and drilling down into the actual capabilities and risks each tool brings to the table and how they might drive progress toward the ultimate goal—or set things back.
• Develop guardrails: Once executives understand the technologies they want to integrate into their workflows to drive results and the ones employees might turn to on their own to expedite work, they should assemble a cross-functional team to weigh the risks and benefits of different use cases. This team can work to outline best practices for the organization as a whole and communicate them to workers along with their reasoning for implementing the guardrails that will be in place.
• Communicate and adjust: Of course, as technology advances and more employees become familiar with these tools, new use cases may arise. Leaders should implement a regular review of best practices to ensure that they are keeping up with new tools and new safeguards that software developers integrate into their products.
It’s important to note that the above is as pressing for leaders in companies that are waiting to integrate AI as it is for those who are already using these tools throughout the enterprise. The fact is that even if the company hasn’t invested in internal AI tools, employees are already using those available online. Undertaking the process outlined above will help leaders ensure that their companies’ use of AI reflects their ethos and values while offering the peace of mind that employees’ use of these tools—no matter how well-intentioned—doesn’t lead to unintended consequences.

title: Council Post: ChatGPT Isn’t A Swiss Army Knife—And Other AI Tips For Agencies
text:
Devin Schumacher is the founder and head of growth of SERP.
While artificial intelligence has been the center of conversations worldwide, it’s far from a new concept in marketing.
In Salesforce’s 2022 State of Marketing report, 68% of marketers indicated that “they have a fully-defined AI strategy,” which represents a “steady climb from 60% in 2021 and 57% in 2020.” What’s more, HubSpot’s report, The State of AI in Marketing in 2023, found that “67% of marketers who use AI use it to create content faster,” and 60% “say generative AI has been most helpful for creating social media posts, followed by product descriptions (50%), and emails (43%).”
There are valid concerns about AI’s negative consequences, but the writing on the wall is clear. Companies that want to stay ahead must strategically approach AI, and marketing agencies are no exception. Marketing agencies that fail to understand and adapt to AI risk becoming less efficient and innovative—and losing opportunities to their competitors. Here are four key tips that will help marketing agencies successfully leverage AI to remain competitive.
1. Learn Basic Programming
Marketing agency leaders should invest in resources to teach their teams basic programming skills.
Various AI tools can help marketers with different tasks, such as outlining blog posts and scheduling social posts. For the most part, these tools are designed to be easy to use; people without technical backgrounds can quickly get onboarded. But these out-of-the-box AI tools can only do so much. That’s where basic programming knowledge steps in. If marketers have foundational programming skills, they can leverage AI for more complex tasks, such as stringing together multiple workflows, rather than being confined to the given capabilities existing AI tools present. Marketers don’t need to become programming experts. Learning a commonly used programming language, like Python, is sufficient.
2. Find AI Tools Designed For Specific Use Cases
ChatGPT is the center of the conversation on AI at the moment for good reason—it offers marketers a variety of ways to streamline their work. But ChatGPT is not, and should not, be treated as a Swiss Army knife because it simply isn’t the best solution for every marketing use case.
Marketers should analyze their needs and seek specific AI tools designed to address those use cases. For instance, marketers looking to outline blog posts faster should avoid relying on ChatGPT and explore AI solutions that cater to that function. Marketers can also build their own custom-made tools (depending on their programming skill levels, they might opt to collaborate with developers). Marketers can get better results by using solutions designed for specific use cases.
3. Use AI To Fill Knowledge Gaps, Replace Tedious Tasks And Get Into A Groove
By using AI tools to fill knowledge gaps and replace mundane tasks, marketers can conserve their time, energy and mental power for more high-level initiatives. For instance, AI tools like ChatGPT are great for operational efficiencies, such as generating basic Google Sheets formulas and quickly finding answers to what would otherwise be a drawn-out series of steps.
For instance, when I had to move subdomains from a client’s website, I knew that moving one subdomain at a time would be tedious and inefficient. So, I asked ChatGPT how to move those subdomains in bulk, and once it gave me the instructions, I sent that information to my team. My team used that guidance to quickly move the subdomains over, saving what I estimate to be six days’ worth of work.
AI tools are also great for kickstarting tasks that require a lot of mental energy, such as brainstorming and writing outlines. I don’t think AI should do all the thought work; marketers must still exercise their expertise and best judgment. Rather, I think marketers can use AI to get into a groove and, once they’re on a roll, take things into their own hands by bringing in their knowledge and skills. For example, instead of spending hours trying to brainstorm ideas for a new marketing campaign and hitting dead ends, a marketer could enlist ChatGPT for brainstorming help—and then refine those ideas.
4. Don’t Over-Rely On AI
While more marketers should be using AI, the industry must be mindful of not going too far in the other direction by becoming over-reliant on AI. Like with many other things in life, overusing AI is a bad call.
AI can simplify and streamline many marketing tasks and workflows but can also lead marketers astray if they aren’t careful. Notably, a 2023 study by NewsGuard, a company that checks for online misinformation, found that “the chatbot operating on GPT-4, known as ChatGPT-4, is actually more susceptible to generating misinformation” and “more convincing in its ability to do so” than ChatGPT-3.5. Specifically, NewsGuard ran 100 false narratives and prompts through ChatGPT-4, and the tool “responded with false and misleading claims for all 100 of the false narratives.”
Relying too heavily on ChatGPT and other AI tools could jeopardize marketing initiatives. For instance, if a company’s marketing team uses ChatGPT to write articles for the corporate blog from scratch and doesn’t fact-check any of the claims, it could end up giving customers the wrong information, potentially resulting in lost sales.
Marketers should consider AI tools helpful guides rather than decision-makers with total control. By adopting that mindset, carefully thinking through their AI use cases and developing well-thought-out plans for leveraging AI tools, marketers can ultimately give themselves more time to solve their clients’ challenges in innovative, delightful ways.

title: Council Post: AI And The Doctor-Patient Relationship: What Physicians Should Consider
text:
Dr. Mary Mason is the CEO and founder of Little Medical School.
Physician burnout is a real issue that continues to grow and threatens the quality of medicine and access to healthcare. Not a day goes by without me hearing one of my physician colleagues complain that paperwork and documentation in electronic medical records continue to take up more and more of their time and impact the quality of their patient interactions.
Artificial intelligence (AI) can offer a real solution to the growing paperwork that primary care physicians and specialists must complete daily. With a simple internet search, it is easy to discover numerous apps and IT platforms that use the power of AI to help doctors write history and physicals, discharge summaries and more simply by recording the visit between the doctor and the patient. The value proposition of such applications is to decrease the amount of documentation and charting for healthcare professionals. This can not only allow physicians to reclaim some time for themselves and their families but also spend more time listening and taking care of the patient during a visit.
Several options are available for physicians to access this type of AI tool. Some larger companies offer sophisticated products and support at the organizational level with a high price tag. And then, there are simple apps that a physician can download themselves.
I am a big fan of using AI to improve career satisfaction for physicians who might often feel more like a scribe than a highly trained professional who diagnoses and treats patients. However, as with every new technology finding new uses daily, we must pause and consider the ramifications of introducing such private doctor-patient interactions into an AI engine. As patient data and details of a doctor's visit are fed into the AI engine, the product is learning from this and remembers it.
Here are some questions I believe AI presents when applied to private healthcare information and data that doctors should consider before bringing the technology into an exam room.
1. Do patients know when their private healthcare data is being fed into an AI engine?
Perhaps you have decided to try an AI app on your own to see how it works. After all, transcription systems have been around for years helping healthcare workers transcribe notes for electronic medical records. But new AI applications are a whole different ballgame. You still need to consider the consent process.
I am the first to admit when I go to the doctor's office and am given a stack of HIPPA forms, I sign them without reading the fine print. However, AI and its use during hospital and office visits presents a new wrinkle in the world of patient privacy. Before you ask patients to sign those papers, make it clear to them whether they are consenting to use AI with their personal healthcare information and what that means for their privacy.
2. What happens to patients' health information and data once fed into an AI application?
This question is difficult to answer, as we don't have a crystal ball to see what technology and data access will look like in the future. For example, closed adoptions decades ago promised birth parents would never be disclosed to a child. Yet, today, this information can often be found with a simple DNA saliva test and membership to a genetic testing service. Unfortunately, we have no way to predict how our data will evolve in the future when it's fed into a system that does not have restricted access.
With this in mind, I would encourage physicians to actively participate in committees or task forces reviewing AI-driven clinical applications and carefully evaluating how patient privacy standards are being upheld. Additionally, I recommend reviewing the consent forms your patients are signing, especially if their data is being put into AI applications. Also, make sure the mandatory HIPPA training that hospitals and healthcare organizations’ employees must complete is up to date, especially when it comes to teaching about AI and patient privacy.
3. Who has access to patients' private data in an AI application?
Once again, the rules on who will access your patients' data once fed into an AI-powered product must be clarified. The legal and compliance discussions and regulations have yet to catch up with the momentum of adopting and implementing the technology.
4. What happens to the recording of patient visits that are fed into the AI application?
This is one of my most significant concerns with AI using the recording of the doctor-patient visit to produce medical documentation. This goes beyond asking AI to help you write a 1,000-word essay on a topic, suggest a sightseeing agenda for your next trip or develop a marketing campaign for your business. I believe we must make sure HIPPA standards and compliance apply to all such applications in the healthcare field.
AI presents a great opportunity to revolutionize healthcare and make physicians more productive by reducing the growing burden of medical documentation and allowing them to spend more time with their patients. However, we must understand the legal and ethical ramifications of feeding sensitive medical information into the AI engine. Doctors should ensure patients understand how their private healthcare data will be used, accessed and protected once put into an AI application during an office or hospital visit. And if doctors incorporate these applications into their day-to-day practice, they must ensure that all steps are taken to protect their patients' healthcare information privacy.

title: The Age Of Strikes: Is AI The Business Solution?
text:
In an era when human workers increasingly demand better wages, improved working conditions and respect for their rights, a silent, unyielding force emerges: artificial intelligence. This technological marvel offers efficiency, consistency and 24/7 productivity without the need for breaks, benefits or bargaining. The stark contrast between human workers' demands and AI's tireless output is becoming impossible to ignore.
Amid the backdrop of rapid technological advancements, Hollywood's writers and actors are striking to preserve their identity and creative essence in an industry in which AI threatens to replicate their roles and produce content. Simultaneously, the United Auto Workers' strike against major automakers underscores the vulnerabilities of industries still dependent on human labor, especially with looming AI-driven automation. Both strikes highlight the growing tension and existential crisis faced by human workers as AI's capabilities expand, raising questions about the future relevance of human contributions in various sectors.
While humans, with their emotions and vulnerabilities, protest passionately, AI stands unflinchingly, almost mocking humanity with its unwavering efficiency. It's as if we're witnessing a silent coup, with machines poised to replace roles once cherished by humans.
AI Doesn’t Go on Strike
AI's most evident advantage is its unwavering commitment. Unlike humans, AI doesn’t strike, demand better conditions or seek a fair wage. It performs its tasks without complaint. This dedication benefits industries needing consistent output but raises concerns about human labor's future. If AI can work without the "hassles" of human involvement, where does that leave us?
AI Keeping Industries Moving Forward
The auto industry's reliance on human labor has often been a double-edged sword. While humans bring skill and adaptability, they also bring vulnerabilities, such as the need for safe working conditions and fair wages, often leading to strikes. AI, with its robotic counterparts, offers a solution to these challenges. Robots can tirelessly work, unaffected by the physical and mental strains that humans endure. They can operate in environments that might be hazardous to human workers, ensuring that car production doesn't stall even when labor disputes arise.
On the other hand, Hollywood's intricate blend of creativity and technical prowess is being challenged by AI's capabilities. While the human touch has always been at the heart of storytelling, AI systems today can analyze vast amounts of data, from audience preferences to historical film successes, to generate scripts that resonate. Furthermore, AI tools in post-production can rapidly edit footage, optimize sound and even create visual effects, ensuring that projects stay on schedule.
Strikes Highlight the Business Need for AI
Strikes, essential for advocating workers' rights, inadvertently underscore the business appeal of AI. For companies, the allure of uninterrupted productivity becomes irresistible. It's not merely about replacing humans but ensuring business continuity in a volatile world.
AI Crossroads: Innovation or Annihilation?
Hollywood's future is uncertain. Some see AI as a tool for unmatched innovation, while others view it as the industry's doom.
While the advantages of AI are often lauded, it's essential to recognize its inherent drawbacks. AI systems can sometimes produce hallucinations or misinterpretations, leading to inaccurate outputs. Moreover, AI isn't entirely self-sufficient; human intervention is crucial to guide, refine, and advance these systems. Perhaps most notably, the societal implications of AI can't be ignored. Replacing human workers with machines can lead to public outrage and significant PR challenges.
Hollywood's challenges reflect global industrial dilemmas. As we navigate the intersection of technology and creativity, championing the human spirit is essential.
AI's allure is undeniable, tempting industries with cost savings and unmatched efficiency. However, its influence extends beyond the workplace. From shaping our viewing habits to influencing purchases, AI's impact is pervasive. It's not just job displacement; it's how AI subtly alters our behaviors and perceptions and may even influence us to strike.

title: Council Post: Rising Threats Demand Innovative Solutions: How To Improve Cybersecurity In Data Centers
text:
Gopi Sirineni serves as President & CEO of Axiado, a cybersecurity processor company securing end-to-end digital infrastructure.
Data centers stand as prominent targets for cybercriminals due to their abundant collection of critical information. These assets encompass personal and financial records, intellectual property and confidential trade secrets, all of which become accessible if cyberthieves breach the digital fortifications protecting them.
Recognizing the allure of valuable data, operators of these centers must deploy robust security measures and protocols to thwart attacks and uphold the confidentiality of client data. However, despite progress in security technology, instances of ransomware and other forms of cyberattacks are on the rise, underscoring the vulnerability of today’s data centers.
In typical ransomware scenarios, malicious actors gain unauthorized access to a system, seize control and demand a ransom. Attackers can exploit vulnerabilities in various software layers, or “ports of entry,” such as the kernel, firmware, applications and drivers running on hardware. Moreover, physical access to hardware also poses a challenge, as even trusted employees can turn rogue or their credentials can be compromised. While many existing solutions focus solely on software and aim to monitor and safeguard software-based entry points, a more comprehensive approach is necessary.
So Many Tools, So Much Time
Cybercriminals have a wide array of tools at their disposal. Distributed denial of service attacks can overload a data center's servers, causing them to crash and render the data inaccessible. Malware can be used to gain access to data center systems to steal data or damage infrastructure. Threats from within an organization by employees or contractors with access to data center systems can intentionally (or accidentally) harm the data or infrastructure.
After the initial breach, malware continues to attack the targeted system through paths of least resistance, after which the malware can either infiltrate the data center immediately or lie in wait for days, months or years until conditions are right for exploitation.
To Be Secure, Trust Nothing, Verify Everything
With so much at stake and hackers continuously changing their digital camouflage like chameleons, the cybersecurity industry has come to realize that current security applications are inadequate. One solution is to use cybersecurity best practices anchored in "zero trust," a premise that reverses the assumption that anything or anyone inside the network can be trusted. The zero-trust mantra is “Never trust, always verify.” The protocol assumes every potential connection must be verified before it is allowed to communicate with a network device.
In my experience, most zero-trust models rely on hardware-based root-of-trust technology. This approach is excellent for low-level attackers without sophisticated arsenals, like state actors. But if the hardware ROT is compromised, the zero-trust model fails completely, as threat actors now have the master key and can authenticate themselves any number of times.
Improving Your Approach To Zero Trust
To help combat these kinds of attacks, some organizations might turn to artificial intelligence. AI algorithms can process massive amounts of threat intelligence data in near real time and add them to a threat library.
According to a recent IBM data breach report (registration required), the average cost of a data breach reached a record high of $4.45 million in 2023. The report concluded that AI technology had the greatest impact on accelerating the speed of breach identification and containment. Organizations that fully deployed both AI and automation in their cybersecurity approaches typically experienced 108-day shorter data breach lifecycles and significantly lower incident costs compared to organizations without these technologies.
Through my company, which provides an AI-driven hardware security platform, I've seen that AI can help continuously monitor and perform run-time attestation of cloud containers, platform operating systems and firmware. This can create efficiencies that help reduce time spent investigating potential threats. AI engines can also enhance detection by identifying advanced attack patterns that traditional techniques might not detect. Analyzing large amounts of data and identifying subtle patterns are integral to AI-based security. These AI systems learn from known attacks and are able to predict zero-day vulnerabilities and assist existing zero-trust models.
What To Know Before Introducing AI
While integrating AI into cybersecurity offers a promising frontier for digital protection, companies venturing into this realm must be cognizant of several challenges. The initial setup can be costly, encompassing not just the AI solution but also infrastructure and training. While deep AI expertise isn't imperative, a firm understanding of cybersecurity threats, system vulnerabilities and the nuances of managing data lake structures is vital. Employees should be educated about these cybersecurity nuances and trained to recognize threats, such as phishing attacks. The primary responsibility for maintaining this security infrastructure and ensuring its efficient application alongside AI tools rests with the chief information security officer and their team.
Also, the interaction between AI solutions and various cloud service providers necessitates seamless integration, a challenge compounded by the need for cloud providers to collaboratively form a unified database. To help ensure success, companies should invest in training, collaborate closely with AI vendors, launch pilot programs to familiarize their teams with the new systems and continuously update their knowledge to stay abreast of the evolving cybersecurity landscape.
Cybersecurity has become a top priority for all governments and organizations. More effective zero-trust protocols will secure the future of data centers and give peace of mind to our digital communications for years to come.

title: Tech companies try to take AI image generators mainstream with better protections
text:
Artificial intelligence tools that can conjure whimsical artwork or realistic-looking images from written commands started wowing the public last year. But most people don't actually use them at work or home.
That could change as leading tech companies are competing to mainstream the use of text-to-image generators for a variety of tasks, integrating them into familiar tools such as Microsoft Paint, Adobe Photoshop, YouTube and ChatGPT.
But first, they're trying to convince consumers, business users and government regulators that they've tamed some of the Wild West nature of early AI image-generators with stronger safeguards against copyright theft and troubling content.
A year ago, it was a relatively small group of early adopters and hobbyists playing with cutting-edge image generators such as Stable Diffusion, Midjourney and OpenAI's DALL-E.
“The previous ones were an interesting curiosity,” but businesses were wary, said David Truog, an analyst at market research group Forrester.
Then came the backlash, including copyright lawsuits from artists and photo stock company Getty, and calls for new laws to rein in generative AI technology's misuse to create deceptive political ads or abusive sexual imagery.
Those problems aren't yet resolved. But now there's a proliferation of new image generators from makers who say they're business-ready this time.
“Alexa, create an image of cherry blossoms in the snow,” is the kind of prompt that Amazon says U.S. customers will be able to speak later this year to generate a personalized display on their Fire TV screen.
Adobe, known for the Photoshop graphics editor it introduced more than three decades ago, was the first this year to release an AI generator designed to avoid legal and ethical problems created by competitors who trained their AI models on huge troves of images pulled off the internet.
“When we talk to customers about generative technology, mostly what we hear is a lot of the technology is really cool, but they don’t feel like they can use it because of these questions,” said Adobe’s chief technology officer, Ely Greenfield.
That's why Adobe's product, called Firefly, was built on its own Adobe Stock image collection, as well as content it has license to use. Stock contributors also are getting some compensation out of the arrangement, Greenfield said.
“Adobe Firefly is clean legally, whereas the others are not," said Truog, the Forrester analyst. “You don’t really care about that if you’re just some dude having fun with generative AI.”
But if you’re a business or a creative professional thinking about using images on your website, apps, or in print layouts, advertising or email marketing campaigns, “it’s kind of a big deal,” Truog said. “You don’t want to be getting into trouble.”
Some competitors are taking note. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI unveiled its third-generation image generator DALL-E 3 on Wednesday, emphasizing both its impressive capabilities, its future integration with ChatGPT and new safeguards to decline requests that ask for an image in the style of a living artist. Creators can also opt their images out from training future models, though Truog notes that OpenAI hasn't said anything “about compensating authors whose work they use for training, even with permission.”
In separate New York City showcase events Thursday, both Microsoft and Google-owned YouTube also unveiled new products infused with AI image generation.
Microsoft, a major investor in OpenAI, showed how it is already starting to bake DALL-E 3 into its graphics design tools, mostly for background editing, as well as its Bing search engine and chatbot. YouTube revealed a new Dream Screen for short YouTube videos that allows creators to compose a new background of their choosing.
——
AP business writers Cora Lewis and Haleluya Hadero contributed to this report.

title: Zelenskyy's final message
text:
Zelenskyy’s final message
Presented by Philip Morris International
With Nahal Toosi and Mona Zhang
POLITICO’s Global Insider is morphing this week into UNGA Playbook, an exclusive seven-edition series spotlighting the world stage at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. But that’s just the start! We’re thrilled to announce the upcoming evolution of this newsletter into POLITICO’s Global Playbook. This premier pop-up newsletter, authored by Suzanne Lynch, is an insider’s look at the pivotal gatherings and moments shaping global policy, politics, and power. Up next: The frontlines of COP28 from Dubai in November. Stay tuned!
Follow Suzanne on X | Send tips to [email protected]
Good morning from New York. I’m Suzanne Lynch, bringing you Thursday’s edition of U.N. Playbook. Keep sending your tips and info here as we keep you up to date on what’s happening this week at the U.N. General Assembly, where some of the biggest players in politics, industry and civil society meet for high-level debates on the climate, health and development challenges facing the world right now.
ZELENSKYY’S PARTING SHOT
MOVING TRIBUTE: On Wednesday night, in the stunning surroundings of the Cipriani on Wall Street, Volodymyr Zelenskyy delivered his final message to the New York crowd as he prepared to depart the city for Washington: Don’t give up on Ukraine.
Details: The Ukrainian president, fresh from a series of meetings at U.N. headquarters after delivering a speech at the Security Council, struck an incongruous note, dressed in his trademark khaki T-shirt amid the glitz and glamor of the Atlantic Council Global Citizen Awards event.
But his message and sincerity was unmistakable. “I address this award to all Ukrainian men and women in uniform. I address this award to all our sweet children who have been killed by Russian terrorists — I will never forget them,” he told the audience of prime ministers, C-suite corporate execs and civil society activists. “I address this award to our fathers [and] mothers who brought up [such] brave Ukrainian soldiers. And to all teachers and to all doctors who didn’t leave the Ukraine from [the] first days of full-scale war.”
Next stop Washington: Zelenskyy may have spent the past 36 hours focused on winning over non-Western countries that have been equivocal about their support for the Ukrainian cause, but today his focus will be on the U.S. as he travels to Washington. One of his tasks? Convincing wavering Republicans that they should continue to provide funds and weapons to Ukraine (among his engagements is a meeting with House Speaker Kevin McCarthy). He is also expected to visit the Pentagon. (The visit comes just after another ally, Poland, announced it is no longer sending weapons to Kyiv.)
Message for U.N.: Zelenskyy pulled no punches in his speech to the Security Council Wednesday — but his target was not so much Russia as it was the United Nations itself. As Nahal, Eric Bazail-Eimil and Mona write, the Ukrainian leader slammed the international body’s ineffectiveness in the face of Russia’s war on Kyiv in a tension-filled special session.
547 days and counting … since full-fledged Russian aggression means “547 reasons for changes in this chamber,” he said, telling the Security Council that it was time to reform. “Veto power in the hands of the aggressor has pushed the U.N. into deadlock.”
Telling it as it is: He wasn’t the only one to slam the Security Council. “Let’s not beat around the bush. Russia’s unprovoked invasion of Ukraine has once again shown the inability of the Security Council to act,” said Austria’s Foreign Minister Alexander Schallenberg. “It’s high time that we address the obvious structural problems.”
Close encounter: In the end, a head to head between Zelenskyy and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov never happened. Lavrov arrived after Zelenskyy left.
Security Council marathon: The action will continue today at the U.N.’s key decision-making body, with Wednesday’s debate due to spill over because of the number of speakers on the list.
Diplomat of the day: Albanian Prime Minister (and former basketball star) Edi Rama, who shut down Russian Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia’s complaints about Ukraine’s inclusion with this one-line riposte: “There is a solution for this. If you agree you will stop the war, President Zelenskyy will not take the floor.” And threw in a bit of Russian literary history to boot.
“Who is the aggressor and who is the aggressed? It is the same sharp difference between war and peace, as Tolstoy would remind you. Go back and read it.”
RAGING WITH THE MACHINES
HELLO AI: As some of the world’s biggest political names battle it out over politics, climate action and Sustainable Development Goals, there’s another theme permeating the debates here at UNGA — artificial intelligence.
Big picture: New technologies like ChatGPT have rocked the world this year, and AI has been on the tip of leaders’ tongues this week amid concerns about the impact on jobs, security and the technology’s potential to widen the gap between advanced and developing economies.
U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken and others discussed how to use AI to actually improve lives during a high-level meeting Monday … South Korea’s President Yoon Suk Yeol called for an international organization to govern the use of AI in his speech to the Security Council …. Even Ukraine’s Zelenskyy referenced AI in his U.N. address, warning it could be used for combat, before it’s harnessed to help humanity.
Thinking ahead: Policy-makers gathered here are discussing ways to harness AI and distribute it equitably — from helping to predict climate patterns (which has become all the more urgent given this month’s floods in Libya) to using AI to help document the war damage in Ukraine. “What we don’t want is this to become like Covid vaccines — that the developing world is left behind,” said one diplomat.
What we’re hearing: Playbook heard from some key figures in the AI community about the chatter this week:
Google’s Senior Vice President of Research, Technology and Society James Manyika:
“There’s a lot of talk about AI in every setting … On the one hand there’s a lot of discussions about what are the possibilities, what progress has been made and could this help advance the SDGs [Sustainable Development Goals]; on the other, when you have representatives of the entire world here, you quickly realize that the conversations in the Global South are different than the conversation in many Western economies. The question of inclusivity — how does everyone participate, how we make sure all countries are part of the conversation, is crucial.”
Botswana’s Foreign Minister Lemogang Kwape, on making sure the AI dividend is spread equally:
“Young people represent 60 percent of our population … We need to invest in them, and in their creativity … There’s a need to regulate, but in regulating they must not impede creativity. We must make sure people remain creative. By being creative, they solve a lot of problems. We have to find that right balance.”
Brad Smith of Microsoft, on why the digital divide is broader than just AI:
“Every UNGA week, every year, we have fundamentally a variant on the same conversation. What do we do about a world that has such an extraordinary divide between the North and the South?” he told an SDG panel. “A critical reason is because technology did not diffuse on a truly global basis. Consider this: 41 years ago this month, the first building in Manhattan, The New York Times building, was lit by electricity, and yet this morning, there were 600 million people in Africa — 43 percent of an entire continent — that woke up with no access to electricity. If we’re going to advance connectivity, if we’re going to advance AI, we have to advance all the technologies together, close the connectivity gap.”
HAPPENING TODAY
HEALTH CARE FOR ALL: The high-level health meetings continue today with a gathering of a dozen government leaders and international organizations focusing on universal health coverage, reports my colleague Carmen Paun.
Real world reminder: More than half of the world’s population doesn’t have coverage for essential health services, the World Health Organization and the World Bank said in a report this week — and 2 billion people face severe financial hardship when paying out-of-pocket for health services and products.
What to expect: The leaders of Chile, Congo and Switzerland are among the 12 heads of state expected to speak.
The meeting is expected to result in a political declaration with more than 100 points, including concerns about the high prices of some health products and inequitable access to them within and among countries.
Russian obstruction: At the first high-level health meeting of the week on Wednesday (which was focused on pandemics), leaders preliminarily approved a joint declaration that ensures access to medicine and vaccines, strengthens disease surveillance and bolsters the work of the WHO.
But opposition from Russia and its allies threatens adoption by the General Assembly in October, POLITICO’s Evan Peng reports. The bloc of nearly a dozen countries is using the opportunity to express their opposition to the use of certain economic sanctions.
SEEN AND HEARD
AROUND TOWN
MEN IN BLACK: “This morning’s commute looked a little different,” tweeted Matthew Miller, U.S. State Department spokesperson, on Wednesday, linking to a picture of Blinken and his posse crossing midtown Manhattan. Yes, different alright — six suited men but no sign of a woman anywhere in his orbit. Maybe time to shake things up?
BEST DRESSED: U.S. Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen sporting a high-collared, zebra-print suit jacket as she received the Atlantic Council Global Citizen Award at the Cipriani, Wall Street last night.
REACHING OUT: There’s lots of talk this week about bridging the divide between North and South. Yesterday, the Nordic countries in the EU held a breakfast with Latin American representatives — more bilaterals are planned with African, Asian and Caribbean countries in the coming days.
Smaller countries unite: One point that Playbook is picking up on the sidelines is that the Biden “democracy versus autocracy” argument against Russia doesn’t necessarily wash with a lot of the countries in the U.N. that are, well … autocracies. What does resonate is the argument — particularly with former colonized nations — that a country should not be permitted to invade its neighbor.
Speaking after Wednesday’s breakfast, Finland’s Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen said part of her objective this week is communicating the impact of her country’s own experience, as a small, independent country that has been subject to Russian aggression in the past. “Finland as a small nation can bring our experience to the table. In the past we’ve had to defend our country against illegal invasion by Russia, the Soviet Union back then,” she explained.
“Luckily we remained independent, but the Finnish people can sympathize with Ukraine. If the world was a place where the bigger power would decide everything then it would be a much worse place for everybody.”
TOP TIPS
— Chill-out zone: Take some time away from the madness and step into the Qatari Salon at U.N. headquarters. Air-conditioning, comfy seats and understated decor — that’s if you have the sufficiently high-ranking accreditation badge to make it in (otherwise you’ll need an escort).
— Reconnect with nature … by popping into the SDG Pavilion on the north lawn of the U.N. complex. Its foliage-themed interior and relaxed vibe is more indie-chic than international diplomacy but the conversation there is compelling.
— Take the subway: Full marks to Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who’s been using the subway to criss-cross New York City. Really, it’s the only way to navigate this week.
— Grab your AirPods … and download the first episode of Power Play, POLITICO’s brand new podcast. In an interview with host Anne McElvoy, Keir Starmer, the man who wants to be Britain’s next prime minister, says he’ll restore the U.K.’s “reputation on the world stage.”
“I feel very strongly that since Brexit, there’s been a sense that we’ve not just exited the EU, that we’ve somehow turned our back on the world and wherever you go, people feel almost the absence of the U.K., once a leading voice, now rarely consulted,” the U.K. opposition Labour Party leader said.

title: The AI Wars Between Microsoft And Google: 8 Lessons For Entrepreneurs
text:
The first shot has been fired. The AI war has begun.
Microsoft’s opening salvo in the AI wars is directly aimed at Google. By forming a strategic partnership with OpenAI. Satya Nadella has orchestrated a seismic shift in the search world by combining OpenAI’s ChatGPT and expansive language model into Bing, Microsoft’s search engine.
So, what are the crucial lessons from Microsoft’s bold declaration of war to dominate search and its potential ramifications? What are the implications of this first battle of the AI Wars?
Lessons for Entrepreneurs
· Develop platforms in emerging unicorn industries. Platforms offer a way to benefit from multiple streams of revenues, reduce risk, and gain domination.
· Partner with leading-edge companies if you can. And be willing to pay for it. Microsoft invested billions in the partnership with OpenAI, although a lot of it was used to pay itself for the equipment. The results so far have been astounding.
· Prove your technology. Nadella was asked about how he decided to “go all in.” Nadella noted that he was in when he saw that ChatGPT was able to translate the poetry of Rumi into English while maintaining the integrity of the original poetry, which is very difficult. This proof of ChatGPT is also consistent with the 4 Aha’s of Unicorn-Entrepreneurship. The second Aha is proof of Technology, and Nadella moved forward when he saw this proof. Now he is working on the third Aha, which is Strategy Aha, i.e., he needs to find the right strategy to achieve his goals, which is to dominate search.
· Focus. The mistake that many entrepreneurs make is in thinking they can reduce their risk by diversifying. What they do not realize is that diversification is for risk-reducing financiers – not entrepreneurs. Entrepreneurs do not have the time, resources, or bandwidth to go to two wars and win. Interestingly, Nadella thought the same way – even with the vast resources of Microsoft at his disposal. Rather than pursuing five foundational models, he focused on the one that “captures the imagination of the world.”
· Hit the enemy where it hurts. Nadella focused on search where it is a distant second to Google, and it seems to have shaken Google.
· Help everyone develop skills. Nadella’s goal is mind boggling – it is to help everyone become a developer. He cites the example of an Indian entrepreneur who used one of the early GPT versions to build an app that helps farmers use their cell phones to fill out all the government documents in a language they do not know – and get government subsidies to survive and succeed.
· Never quit. Nadella tried to succeed in search at Microsoft, starting about 14 years ago. Now he is trying again with a new technology. And this time he may draw blood, Google’s blood.
The final lesson for entrepreneurs: If you want a chance to build your unicorn, get into an emerging industry as it emerges. Every billion-dollar entrepreneur I have financed, interviewed, or researched entered an emerging industry. An emerging industry creates many growth opportunities.
Lesson for Google.
· You are never safe. It is noteworthy that Microsoft is going to the heart of Google’s empire – search. Just because Google has a 90% market share does not mean that Microsoft cannot make a dent.
· Attack Microsoft where it can really hurt. Sundar Pichai is now facing perhaps the most important fight of his life and he seems to be playing a cautious game. He should take the fight to Microsoft’s heart and prevent them from using all their profits from the cloud, servers, and business software. Find a way to reduce Microsoft’s profits in these areas. Dell started to sell printer cartridges because they wanted to take the fight to HP.
MY TAKE: Will AI help improve the world’s standard of living like the PC and the Internet, or is this the start of Armageddon? Satya Nadella of Microsoft is said to be ecstatic that he beat Google to the launch of an AI product that has captured the imagination of the masses and helped Bing to narrow the gap with Google. But he has also unleashed the AI wars. Google’s co-founder and leading thinker, Larry Page, seems to think that anyone who is cautious about the potential of AI robots controlling humans is a “speciesist” because we should also be concerned about the rights of the robots (really?). And VCs are eagerly looking forward to the billions they will be making – while financing a potentially lethal weapon.
So, what can go wrong?

title: Here’s everything Microsoft announced at its Surface and Copilot event in New York
text:
Microsoft on Thursday unveiled new Surface computers and shared details on the release of this year's version of Windows 11, including its embedded Copilot AI assistant, during an event in New York.
The company introduced the Surface Laptop Studio 2 and the Surface Laptop Go 3, and unveiled enterprise availability for Microsoft 365 Copilot, its supplemental AI tool for core productivity apps like Word and Excel.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella began the event by speaking about how the company's Copilot AI tools will make a broad impact across its user base for consumers and enterprises.
"I mean, it's crazy," he said. "It's kind of like the 90s are back. It's exciting to be in a place where we're bringing some software innovation and really having fun enjoying this entire journey."
Rivals such as Atlassian, Google and Salesforce have also been racing to update their existing products with generative AI this year.
The Surface Laptop Studio 2 starts at $1,999, while the Surface Laptop Go 3 starts at $799. Both will ship with Microsoft's revamped Windows 11 operating system, which includes its Copilot software. The new Surface models will be available Oct. 3 and are available for pre-order today, Microsoft said.
Notably absent from the event was Panos Panay, the Microsoft executive who presented Surface computers to the public for a decade. On Monday Microsoft announced a series of leadership changes as it disclosed that Panay was leaving.
Here's a rundown of Thursday's news:
Windows 11 update
Microsoft said it will begin rolling out the next major update to Windows 11 on Sept. 26.
The update will include the new Copilot in the Bing search engine and the Edge web browser, and people will be able to summon the Copilot by holding down the Windows key and pressing the C key.
Aaron Woodman, VP of Windows marketing at Microsoft, said bringing Copilot to the operating system will be significant because it will make AI accessible to people who might not have worked with it before."I think a lot of what we've seen so far has been kind of inside the tech bubble," Woodman said, while "Windows is a product that reaches a significant portion of the planet."
Here are some of the key features of the new version:
- Boot to the cloud. If you're running a cloud-based version of Windows, you'll be able to log directly into the cloud instance as your primary experience on the your PC, Microsoft said.
- Smarter snipping. It's getting easier to pull out text directly from screenshots with Windows. When using the Snipping Tool app, you can copy text from a screenshot and quickly redact emails or phone numbers.
- Better backup. Microsoft will enable users to back up apps they've previously installed on a PC in order to restore them, along with pinned app preferences, in the future.
- Paint with words. The longstanding Paint app is getting a facelift with help from generative AI. People will be able to type in a few words of text, choose a style and have Paint auto-generate an image matching the description. It's similar to tools from Adobe and other companies, as well as Microsoft's own image creator in the Bing search engine.
- More taskbar customization. Windows 11 introduced a stark new taskbar that puts the Start button and a series of app icons in the center at the bottom of the screen. Now users can view app icons with labels, similar to how things looked in Windows 10. Even apps that aren't running can appear with labels. Users will also be able to hide the time and date.
- Notepad with memory. Notepad will automatically save your status so that if you close the note-taking app and reopen it, you can get right back to your work.
Testers have gotten access to some of these features in early builds in recent months.
Copilot for advertising
Microsoft is also incorporating generative AI into its advertising tool, although the company did not disclose when exactly it will do so. A Copilot for the Microsoft Advertising Platform will be able to answer marketers' questions through a chat interface.
And over time, it will help automate the process of coming up with ads. Alphabet and Meta have both been active in this area.
"Using Copilot in the Microsoft Advertising Platform, you can tailor content, design, and strategies to your branding and advertising goals, creating stunning and effective ads in minutes," Kya Sainsbury-Carter, corporate VP for advertising at Microsoft, wrote in a blog post.
Surface Laptop Studio 2
The Surface Laptop Studio 2 has a similar look and feel to the original model that launched in 2021. It can be used like a traditional laptop with a keyboard, but customers can also lay it flat and use it like a tablet.
It offers a 13th-generation Intel Core chip, with a few options for Nvidia graphics processing units: the GeForce RTX 4050 or 4060, or the RTX 2000 Ada Generation. Models with Nvidia graphics will come with 120-watt power supplies. Or people can choose integrated graphics with Intel Iris Xe.
Microsoft has also added a single traditional USB-A port, along with a MicroSD card reader.
People can choose to include up to 64GB of RAM, compared with a maximum of 32GB in the first iteration.
The device has an 14.4-inch screen and is the "most powerful Surface ever built," Brett Ostrum, Microsoft's VP of Surface devices, said at the event. He added that the Surface Laptop Studio 2 is twice as fast as the previous model, and it also features an updated haptic touchpad, which is the "most inclusive touchpad on any laptop today."
Models with 2TB of storage and Nvidia graphics boast up to 16 hours of battery life, while devices with less space and Nvidia cards can deliver up to 18 hours, while Intel graphics models have a 19-hour capacity, Microsoft said. The company claimed the inaugural Surface Laptop Studio boasted 18 hours of battery life, but CNBC found it generally lasted closer to 4.5 hours.
The new version starts at $1,999, compared with $1,599 for the original model.
Surface Laptop Go 3
The Surface Laptop Go 3 is the latest update to Microsoft's entry-level laptop. It features a 12.4-inch touch screen display and runs on a 12th-generation Intel processor. Ostrum said it's Microsoft's lightest and most portable laptop, weighing in at 2.49 pounds. The Surface Laptop Studio 2 exceeds 4 pounds.
Microsoft said the new laptop's battery will last for 15 hours, compared with 13.5 hours for its predecessor. In terms of performance, the device is 88% faster than the original model, Ostrum said.
People can choose to add up to 16GB of RAM and up to 512GB of solid-state storage, instead of a 8GB memory limit and up to 256GB in solid-state storage in the Surface Laptop Go 2.
The laptop starts at $799, an increase from the $599 starting price of the Surface Laptop Go 2.
Surface Go 4
Microsoft announced the Surface Go 4, the latest miniature version of its Surface Pro tablet that's available exclusively for organizations. The company suggested in a release that the new model could be especially useful for businesses and frontline workers.
The Surface Go 4 can be docked to a monitor, used as a laptop with a paired keyboard or like a tablet using the touch screen.
It's powered by an Intel N200 processor. The Surface Go 4 also features an 10.5-inch touchscreen display and supports 12.5 hours of battery life, which is an increase from the 11 hours of battery life offered by the Surface Go 3.
Surface Hub 3
Microsoft hasn't forgotten about its Surface Hub, its large touchscreen device for use in the office.
A 85-inch model and a smaller 50-inch option offer organizations an easy way to join Teams video calls. During Teams calls, software will be able to remove the background from various participants and adjust their sizes, Microsoft product marketing director Frank Buchholz wrote in a blog post.
The smaller version can switch between portrait and landscape modes. Two people can simultaneously draw or write on the devices with Surface Hub Pens or Surface Slim pens.
Microsoft is touting 60% better performance in the main processor of these devices and a 160% bump for their graphics processing units.
Microsoft 365 Copilot release for big businesses
Large organizations will be able to start paying for Microsoft 365 Copilot starting Nov. 1.
The launch could provide a financial boost to Microsoft 365, formerly known as Office 365, a key part of the business that had 382 million commercial seats in the fiscal third quarter. Microsoft said enterprises can call their account representatives to get started.
Companies that participated in the tool's early access program will be given first chance to deploy the software, which will cost $30 per person per month on top of Microsoft 365's existing costs. Microsoft has also started allowing some small businesses into the early access program.
"In the testing that we've already done with preview customers, you're in a meeting, you can have a meeting summary, and the AI can summarize the entire meeting and give it to you in bite-sized chunks, Yusuf Mehdi, the new head of Surface and Windows at Microsoft, told CNBC's Steve Kovach.
"If you missed the meeting, you can tell me what happened out of it, you can say to get action items, what did my boss say, when was I mentioned, and you can get all that. That time is unbelievably precious, and for $30 a month, it's an incredible value. People really love that capability."

title: Nvidia, other US chip stocks stall over valuation, industry worries - ET Telecom
text:
- Devices
- 3 min read
Nvidia, other US chip stocks stall over valuation, industry worries
As the stocks rose this year, so did valuations. At the end of July, the 21-stock S&P 500 semiconductors and semiconductors equipment industry group was trading at 28.5 times forward 12-month earnings estimates, compared to its 10-year average P/E of 16.5 times, according to LSEG Datastream.
By Lewis Krauskopf
NEW YORK: Some of the shine is wearing off shares of Nvidia and other U.S. semiconductor companies after a stunning 2023 rally, as investors weigh steep valuations, rising Treasury yields and signs of industry unease.
Chip stocks soared to start the year, with the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index rising over 50% through July. No stock symbolized the chip industry's success more than Nvidia, whose shares tripled in 2023 as the company's market value topped $1 trillion, driven by excitement over the central role of the company's products in artificial intelligence applications.
But performance for the group has stalled. The SOX semiconductor index is off over 7% this month, versus a 2.3% drop for the broad S&P 500, while shares of Nvidia - a driver of the broader market's rally this year - have declined more than 14% in September.
"They have definitely lost some momentum," said King Lip, chief investment strategist at Baker Avenue Wealth Management. "Many of these chip names got that AI boost. Some of that fervor has kind of simmered down."
As the stocks rose this year, so did valuations. At the end of July, the 21-stock S&P 500 semiconductors and semiconductors equipment industry group was trading at 28.5 times forward 12-month earnings estimates, compared to its 10-year average P/E of 16.5 times, according to LSEG Datastream.
Even with this month's declines, the group still trades at a forward P/E of 23.5 times.
"Coming out of the pandemic and with this rise in popularity and race for AI-related innovation, that created a tailwind for semiconductor stocks," said Kevin Mahn, president and chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh Asset Management.
With "some of the names that really have catapulted to the top, now you are starting to question valuations," Mahn said.
Valuations are coming under further pressure from the rise in Treasury yields. Higher yields on Treasuries - which are seen as virtually risk free - offer investment competition to equities, viewed as a riskier asset class.
Yields jumped on Wednesday, with two-year yields hitting 17-year highs, after the Federal Reserve signaled a policy of interest rates staying higher for longer.
Nvidia's recent weakness has come even after it far exceeded expectations with its revenue forecast when it reported quarterly results in late August. Other big semiconductor stock decliners in September include Lam Research down 12%, and Applied Materials and KLA Corp, both off about 10%.
Interest in the AI sector from retail investors is also waning, according to VandaTrack, which tracks retail activity.
Industry-specific issues are weighing on the group as well, investors said, including ongoing tensions between the United States and China over semiconductors. Washington is considering restrictions on sales of AI microchips, following export controls last year to cut China off from certain semiconductor chips made anywhere in the world with U.S. equipment.
In another blow, Reuters reported on Friday that Taiwan's TSMC has told its major suppliers to delay the delivery of high-end chipmaking equipment, as the world's top contract chipmaker grows increasingly nervous about customer demand. Shares of several TSMC suppliers fell after the report.
Meanwhile, the early buzz following last week's initial public offering of Arm Holdings has worn off, with shares of the chip designer down for a fifth straight day.
Of course, many chip stocks are sitting on substantial gains for the year and this month may only be a temporary setback.
Investors should look for dividend-paying chip companies with strong balance sheets trading at reasonable valuations, said Mahn, whose firm holds shares of Analog Devices and Broadcom.
"I do believe there are opportunities in semiconductor stocks going forward," Mahn said.
